title: Oral and anal detection of Treponema pallidum DNA among transgender women and travestis with high-titre syphilis in Brazil: findings from the MyTTrA study
abstract: Data on transgender women and(TGW) concerning oral and anal detection of(TP) DNA are lacking. We aimed to estimate the prevalence of oral and anal TP DNA detection and the frequency of azithromycin resistance-associated mutations among TGW with high-titre syphilis in Brazil. We conducted a nested cross-sectional study as part of the TransOdara study among TGW in five Brazilian cities. Participants with high-titre syphilis (reactive treponemal test and VDRL titre ≥1:8) and an analysable oral or anal specimen underwent quantitative PCR targeting theandgenes to detect TP DNA. TP DNA-positive specimens were further analysed using nested PCR and Sanger sequencing to identify mutations associated with azithromycin resistance. Among the 249 participants with high-titre serological syphilis and analysable sample, TP DNA was detected in 25 (10.0%, 95% CI 6.6-14.5): 14 (5.6%) from the oral site only, 6 (2.4%) from the anal site only, and 5 (2.0%) from both sites. Participants in whom TP DNA was detected were younger and more frequently reported STI symptoms and anogenital ulcers during the preceding six months. The detection rate increased with VDRL titre (odds ratio 2.44, 95% CI 1.74-3.41 per doubling of titre for any oral or anal detection). Mutations associated with azithromycin resistance were observed in 76% (19/25, 95% CI 54.9-90.6) of participants in whom TP was detected. TP DNA was detected in 10% of participants with high-titre serological syphilis. Detection increased with higher VDRL titres, supporting an association between higher non-treponemal titres and mucosal TP DNA detection. These findings support continued epidemiological and molecular surveillance of syphilis and of azithromycin resistance in transgender populations. They do not support site-specific PCR screening: syphilis diagnosis remains serological, and benzathine benzylpenicillin G remains the treatment of choice. title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

Comprehensive safety and toxicity evaluation of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum LMT1-48, a potential probiotic strain isolated from Kimchi
abstract: Probiotics are widely commercialized as key ingredients in functional foods and dietary supplements; however, ensuring their safety is critical for consumers. In particular, safety must be carefully evaluated at the strain level, as both efficacy and potential risks can vary between strains. In this study, the safety of a novel probiotic strain,LMT1-48, was comprehensively evaluated using phenotypic, genomic, and toxicity studies. Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) values of all tested antibiotics were lower than the cut-off values of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) guidelines.LMT1-48 did not exhibit hemolytic activity nor cytotoxicity. Production of harmful metabolites is also evaluated. The whole genome sequencing did not reveal any antibiotic resistance- or virulence-related genes. Neither single- nor repeated-dose oral toxicity studies have shown any treatment-related toxicological changes at any dose level. Overall, our results suggest thatLMT1-48 is a safe probiotic strain for human consumption.

title: Advances in natural product inhibitors targeting the type III secretion system 1 of Salmonella
abstract: is an important foodborne pathogen that poses significant threats to human health, animal production, and food safety. Increasing antimicrobial resistance and limitations of conventional control strategies have promoted the development of anti-virulence approaches targeting bacterial virulence factors. The type III secretion system 1 (T3SS-1) mediatesinvasion into host cells and effector protein translocation, yet is dispensable for bacterial survival, rendering it a promising anti-virulence target. This review summarizes recent advances in natural product-derived T3SS-1 inhibitors, classifies relevant inhibitors based on chemical structural characteristics and, from a mechanistic perspective, distinguishes direct protein binding mode with well-defined molecular interactions from indirect regulation mode that exert modulatory effects. It further explores the structure-activity relationships (SAR) between the structural features of natural products and their anti-virulence activities, aiming to provide theoretical bases for the discovery and optimization of novel anti-virulence lead compounds.

title: Organic amendments and antibiotic resistance gene diversity in tropical agroecosystems of Réunion Island: an exploratory study
abstract: Environmental reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) are increasingly recognized as important components of One Health surveillance. We explored antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) across agricultural environments on Réunion Island using high-throughput qPCR targeting 349 ARGs in 16 samples comprising manure, soils, water and vegetables. ARGs were widespread, with the highest richness and relative abundance in manure-amended soils and manure. ARG abundance was on average approximately 5-fold higher in amended than paired control soils. Among 60 ARGs classified as high risk to human health, 52 were detected, including 16 in water and 22 in raw vegetables. ARG profiles differed primarily among matrices. Antibiotic residues were detected in only five samples, and neither their occurrence nor Cu/Zn concentrations consistently mirrored ARG patterns. This exploratory screening identifies organically amended soils as compartments of particular interest and provides a baseline for targeted One Health surveillance of environmental AMR in tropical agroecosystems.

Extended spectrum beta lactamases and carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli in humans, animals and the environment in East Africa: a scoping review
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is escalating in East Africa through close human-animal-environment interactions. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) and carbapenemase-producingare clinically critical pathogens, yet local evidence is limited. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on ESBL and carbapenemase-producingin East Africa to inform One Health AMR control strategies. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched, identifying 279 records published between 2015 and 2025. After removing duplicates and screening, 185 articles were assessed for eligibility; 154 studies spanning human, animal and environmental sources met the inclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently extracted epidemiological, microbiological and molecular data in Covidence, including resistance genes and transmission evidence. The 154 included studies spanned 11 East African countries, led by Ethiopia ( = 55), Tanzania ( = 39) and Uganda ( = 22). Most studies (85.7%) were cross-sectional and human-focused (68.2%), with only 19 (12.3%) using a multi-sector One Health design. Overall, 21,554isolates were recovered from 74,700 samples. ESBL prevalence was reported in 117 studies (76.0%, median 46.8%) and carbapenemase prevalence in 65 (42.2%, median 3.3%), representing heterogeneous study-level estimates.predominated (89.9%), led by(26.1%); reported carbapenemase genes included,,andWhole-genome sequencing in 30 studies (19.5%) identified high-risk clones ST131, ST10, ST38 and ST410, though animal, food-chain and environmental sectors remained underrepresented. title: Dietary licorice improves carcass yield, hepatocellular protection, gut health, oxidative status, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens
abstract: Over the past decade, phytotherapy such as licorice has attracted research as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters in broiler production, driven by rising concerns over antimicrobial resistance. However, the consistency of its effects across productive, physiological, and health outcomes remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized published experimental evidence on the effects of dietary licorice on growth performance, carcass yield, blood indices, visceral organs, oxidative status, intestinal morphology, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens. A systematic literature search identified studies published between 2010 and 2025, and effect sizes were computed (Hedges'; 95% confidence interval). Pooled estimates were derived under the random-effects model using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, with between-study heterogeneity characterized bythe-statistic. Univariable mixed-effects meta-regression was conducted to identify study-level moderators of treatment response, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and the Rosenberg fail-safe N criterion. Dietary licorice did not affect feed intake or the feed conversion ratio, but it did increase body weight gain (BWG; SMD = 0.289; = 0.002), breast, thigh, gizzard, and bursa weights ( < 0.05). Gut integrity also improved with the villus height/crypt depth ratio (SMD = 0.931; = 0.041), andspp. counts (SMD = 0.266; = 0.003) increased, whilepopulations were suppressed (SMD = -1.737; < 0.001). Overall, the findings support that licorice enhances body weight gain, with route, duration, sex, and strain moderating efficacy.

abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

Five years of wastewater surveillance reveal COVID-19-Associated amplification and seasonal shifts in bla (KPC) and bla (NDM)
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Intra-DNA k-mer conservation patterns encode evolutionary selection of variants
abstract: Current approaches to variant effect prediction center on protein function and interspecies conservation, largely ignoring cues embedded in local nucleotide composition. We developed kGain, a metric that quantifies how a point mutation reshapes oligonucleotide frequency relative to the host genome. Inandlong-term evolution data, fixed, essential-gene, and recurrent mutations carry elevated kGain values that grow more pronounced over successive generations. Parallel trends appear in SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and in a bottleneck resistance experiment, where a high-kGainY515N change conferred antibiotic resistance at no detectable fitness cost. A transformer regressor trained on one strain transfers accurately to others, indicating that the compositional rules kGain captures are broadly conserved and offering a new sequence-intrinsic dimension for understanding adaptive selection.

Harnessing hydrogel technology for advanced periodontitis therapy: A multifunctional approach to oral health restoration
abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: Bacterial spectrum, age and calendar-quarter distribution, and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of isolates recovered from respiratory specimens of children hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia in Chongqing, China: a three-year retrospective study
abstract: Community acquired pneumonia (CAP) continues to be an important cause of admission of children in hospitals. This study focused on bacterial isolates from respiratory samples, age distribution and antibiotic resistance patterns of children below seven years admitted with CAP in Chongqing, China from January 2023 to December 2025. Of the 2,988 patients included in the study, 884 (29.59%) were positive for bacterial culture, with 930 isolates. The predominant species were Haemophilus influenzae (43.01%), Moraxella catarrhalis (22.80%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (14.84%), and Staphylococcus aureus (10.32%). The distribution of recovered isolates differed significantly across age groups (P < 0.01). After adjustment for calendar year, overall culture positivity did not differ significantly across quarters (P = 0.085), although a significant quarter-by-year interaction was observed (P = 0.005), indicating that quarterly patterns varied between years. Year-adjusted quarterly associations were also observed for H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, and S. aureus. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed high non-susceptibility to ampicillin (65.25%) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (62.33%) among H. influenzae isolates, and to erythromycin and clindamycin (99.19% for each) among S. pneumoniae isolates. Oxacillin non-susceptibility was observed in 20.25% of tested S. aureus isolates, while imipenem non-susceptibility was uncommon among tested Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates. These findings support continued regional microbiological surveillance and may inform institutional antimicrobial stewardship. Because nasotracheal suction specimens may contain colonizing organisms, culture recovery alone does not establish the bacterial causes of CAP.

title: Australian Meningococcal Surveillance Programme Annual Report, 2025
abstract: In Australia, both probable and laboratory-confirmed cases of invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) are reported to the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS). When compared to 2024, the number of IMD notifications in 2025 decreased by 13% to 118. IMD was confirmed by laboratory testing in 115/118 (97%) of 2025 IMD cases, with 66% (76/115) diagnosed by bacterial culture and 34% (39/115) by nucleic acid amplification testing. The genogroup was determined for 93% of laboratory-confirmed cases (107/115): genogroup B (MenB) accounted for 82.2% of infections (88/107); MenW and MenY for 7.5% of disease (8/107) each; MenC for 1.9% (2/107); and MenA for 0.9% (1/107). Finetyping was available for 67% of the cases for which the genogroup was determined (72/107). In MenB isolates, 28 porA types were detected: the most prevalent from amongst these were P1.7-2,4 (21%; 12/58) and P1.7,16-26 (14%; 8/58). Of the eight MenW isolates in 2025, six were finetyped and identified as porA type P1.5,2, MLST (ST) 11 and belonging to the clonal complex 11, the hypervirulent strain reported in outbreaks in Australia and overseas. In MenY infections, four porA types were detected from the five isolates finetyped: P1.21,16; P1.5,10-1; P1.5-1,10-1; and P1.5-2,10-1, with no dominant porA type detected. One of the two MenC isolates was typed, identifying as P1.5-2,10-1 and the single MenA isolate identified as P1.5-2,10. Peaks of IMD occurred in children aged less than 5 years, in those aged 15-24 years, and in adults aged 25-44 years, accounting for 18% (21/115), 23% (26/115) and 22% (25/115) of laboratory-confirmed cases, respectively. In children aged under 5 years, 100% of IMD (21/21) was MenB; in those aged 15-24 years, 100% of IMD (25/25) was MenB; and in those aged 25-44 years, 82% of IMD (18/22) was MenB, with three MenW cases and one MenC case reported in this age group. IMD was reported in all age groups: < 5 years (18%; 21/115); 5-9 years (5%; 6/115); 10-14 years (2.6%; 3/115); 15-24 years (23%; 26/115); 25-44 years (22%; 25/115); 45-64 years (12%; 14/115); and in those aged 65 years and older (17%; 20/115). Whilst MenB predominated in all age groups, the majority of MenY IMD cases (6/8) were reported in adults aged 65 years and older, among whom it accounted for 6/18 cases (33%). All cultured IMD isolates available for antimicrobial susceptibility testing (n = 76) were tested for ceftriaxone and penicillin. Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values were reported using Clinical Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) interpretative criteria: 8% (6/76) were defined as penicillin resistant (MIC value ≥ 0.5mg/L); 64% (49/76) had intermediate susceptibility to penicillin (MIC values 0.125 and 0.25 mg/L); and 28% (21/76) were susceptible to penicillin (MIC values ≤ 0.064 mg/L). All isolates tested were susceptible to ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin and rifampicin.

title: Defeating Multidrug-Resistant ESKAPEE Pathogens With Polymer Nanomaterials
abstract: The clinical efficacy of antibiotics has progressively declined over the past decades as a consequence of the global spread of antimicrobial resistance, a phenomenon that is particularly pronounced among the so-called ESKAPEE pathogens: Enterococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter species, and Escherichia coli. Collectively, these bacteria are responsible for more than 50% of infection-related deaths worldwide, and multidrug-resistance is highly prevalent among them. This alarming trend poses a critical threat to global public health and underscores the urgent need for innovative therapeutic strategies. One such approach involves the use of polymers as drug delivery systems for both conventional antibiotics and novel antimicrobial compounds, in the form of nanoparticles or polymer prodrugs, to circumvent resistance mechanisms. Other promising strategies are polycations with intrinsic antibacterial activity that act through mechanisms not yet widely exploited and polymers exerting photodynamic and photothermal effects. In this review, we summarize and discuss the current evidence for the efficacy of polymer-based strategies against drug-resistant ESKAPEE infections.

title: Race for Speed: Advances in Rapid Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing across Bacterial and Fungal Pathogens
abstract: Rapid antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) is critical in combating the rising burden of microbial infections and the global threat of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Conventional AST methods, developed decades ago, remain the clinical gold standard and require several days to yield results, hindering timely decision-making and delaying targeted therapy. This review highlights recent phenotypic AST approaches developed since 2020 that leverage advances in microfluidics, sensing modalities, and single-cell analysis to enable rapid monitoring of microbial responses to antimicrobials. These strategies substantially reduce turnaround times, support direct testing of clinical specimens, and facilitate integration with upstream sample preparation and pathogen identification within automated, miniaturized platforms that are compatible with high-throughput workflows. Importantly, several of these technologies are being extended beyond bacterial systems to fungal pathogens, addressing a critical unmet need, as delayed antifungal susceptibility testing (AFST) continues to contribute to high morbidity and mortality. Collectively, these advances underscore the potential of sensor-integrated, rapid AST platforms to transform clinical decision-making, improve antimicrobial stewardship, and mitigate the burden of AMR.

title: Furan π Bridge Strengthens Conformation Locking in Asymmetric D-A-π-D NIR-II AIEgens for High-Efficiency Photothermal/NO Synergistic Therapy
abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) pneumonia represents a critical threat owing to its high mortality and antibiotic resistance. Near-infrared II (NIR-II) fluorescent photothermal therapy (PTT) enables deep-tissue heating but risks incomplete bacterial clearance and thermal damage. Symmetric donor-acceptor-donor (D-A-D) NIR-II molecules often suffer from high molecular weights, low fluorescence, and suboptimal photothermal conversion. Herein, we report asymmetric D-A-π-D NIR-II aggregation-induced emission luminogens (AIEgens) featuring a benzothiopyrylium acceptor, triphenylamine donors, and furan or thiophene as π-bridge. Furan strengthens non-covalent conformation locking while weakening intermolecular π-π stacking, thereby enhancing both fluorescence and photothermal performance. AIEgen 4fop achieves an optimal photothermal conversion efficiency of 84.3% and a NIR-II photoluminescence quantum yield of 2.31% in toluene. To boost antibacterial activity, 4fop was co-encapsulated with the thermally responsive NO donor BNN6 into Pluronic F-127 nanoparticles. In a murine pneumonia model, this nanoplatform substantially reduces bacterial burden, suppresses inflammation through TNF pathway modulation, and promotes lung repair. This work establishes a rational D-A-π-D design strategy and an integrated nanoplatform for the precise treatment of deep-seated drug-resistant infections.

title: Zero-valent iron improves nitrogen removal and reduces antibiotic resistance-related discharge from piggery wastewater at low temperature
abstract: Efficient removal of nitrogen and antibiotic resistance-related pollutants from livestock wastewater remains challenging at low temperatures. In this study, two integrated anaerobic-aerobic biofilm reactors were operated for 203 days at decreasing temperatures of 20 °C-12 °C to evaluate the effects of zero-valent iron (ZVI) on nutrient removal, antibiotic degradation and antibiotic resistance control. Compared with the control reactor, the ZVI-fortified IAOBR maintained higher treatment performance under low-temperature stress. At 12 °C, total nitrogen removal remained at 78.9 % in the ZVI system, compared with 52.5 % in the control. The ZVI system also achieved consistently higher total antibiotic removal efficiencies of 66.1 %-81.8 %, whereas the control achieved only 23.8 %-46.5 %. Mass balance analysis showed that antibiotic removal was dominated by residual mass loss (including biodegradation and abiotic transformation) instead of adsorption. Moreover, ZVI enhanced antibiotic removal by improving iron availability, microbial metabolic activity, electron-transfer capacity and ATP production. ZVI also enriched key nitrogen-removing and antibiotic-degrading bacteria, including Candidatus Brocadia, Comamonas, Hydrogenophaga, Thauera, Pseudomonas and Mycobacterium. However, ZVI promoted ARG and MGE enrichment in biofilms, suggesting that part of the reduction in aqueous-phase ARG abundance could be associated with their retention or enrichment in attached biomass. These findings demonstrate the potential of ZVI-fortified IAOBRs for low-temperature piggery wastewater treatment, while highlighting the need to manage biofilm-associated resistance risks.

title: Optimization of Sulbactam Dosing for Acinetobacter baumannii Meningitis in Adult Patients from a Perspective of Cerebrospinal Pharmacokinetics
abstract: Meningitis caused by Acinetobacter baumannii is extremely difficult to treat with antibacterial chemotherapy because of antimicrobial resistance. This study aimed to conduct a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pharmacokinetic (PK)/pharmacodynamic (PD) evaluation and propose an effective dosing strategy for adult patients from a quantitative perspective. Literature was systematically collected for sulbactam CSF concentration data. A CSF PK model was developed using a model approach that integrates the existing blood PK model with reported serum and CSF concentrations. The CSF PK/PD simulation was conducted to calculate the probability of achieving the PK/PD target of 60% time above the minimum inhibitory concentration (60% T > MIC) in CSF. In total, 43 serum and 45 CSF samples in 21 adult patients from three articles were used for the development of CSF PK modeling. For covariate analysis, CSF protein was incorporated into the CSF-to-serum partition coefficient in the final CSF PK model. The visual predictive checks of the final model in serum and CSF concentrations confirmed no major bias. CSF PK/PD breakpoints of only 8 g/day achieved the target concentration of 4 µg/mL in typical patients with inflammatory meningitis (CSF protein ranged from 129 to 645 mg/dL) and creatinine clearance (CL) of 30 mL/min/1.73 m. Optimized dosing regimens for A. baumannii meningitis were developed based on the degree of meningeal inflammation and renal clearance. Alternative or combination strategies may be needed since it is difficult to achieve PK/PD target attainment in CSF as renal function increases.

title: Form-dependent effects of silicon amendments on antibiotic resistance during vermicomposting: Insights into host bacteria and composting performance
abstract: The persistence and dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in livestock manure raise environmental health concerns and challenge the safe agricultural recycling of organic wastes. Although vermicomposting can stabilize manure and lower ARG loads, residual ARGs and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) in final products remain a dissemination concern. Here, we compared nano-silica (NS), sodium silicate (SS), and silicon dioxide (SD) as silicon amendments to enhance cattle manure vermicomposting while mitigating ARG-related risks. Silicon amendment promoted organic matter degradation, nitrogen transformation, and humification, as indicated by increased humic substances, humic acid, HA/FA ratio, and germination index; low-dose nano-silica (NS1) showed the strongest maturity-enhancing effect. Vermicomposting reduced the relative abundance of ARGs by 53.1% compared with raw cattle manure (RM), while NS1 further decreased the relative abundance of ARGs by 19.3% relative to the vermicomposting control and markedly reduced the relative abundance of dominant ARGs, including sul1, tetA, tetB, and tetW. Meanwhile, NS also decreased the relative abundances of key MGEs, such as IncP_oriT, IncI1_repI1, intI2, and IS26, simplified the ARG-MGE-microbial co-occurrence network, and enriched organic matter-degrading bacterial taxa, such as Streptomyces, Nocardioides, and Agromyces. These findings highlight nano-silica as a promising amendment for reducing ARG persistence and mobility-related risks during vermicomposting, providing a practical strategy for safer manure recycling.

title: Occurrence and characterization of ESBL- and AmpC-producing Escherichia coli in the common tern (Sterna hirundo) and surface water of Bahía Samborombón, Argentina
abstract: This study determined the occurrence and genomic background of ESBL- and AmpC-E. coli in common terns (Sterna hirundo) and surrounding surface water during the non-breeding season in Bahía Samborombón, Argentina, a wetland under strong anthropogenic influence. Two hundred common tern faecal samples and 36 surface water samples were analysed. Antimicrobial resistance phenotypes were determined, and whole-genome sequencing was performed to characterise resistance genes, sequence types (STs), and virulence-associated factors. One ESBL-E. coli isolate from common tern faeces, 12 ESBL- and four AmpC-E. coli from surface water were obtained. The predominant ESBL gene was bla, followed by blaand bla, whereas AmpC production was associated with blaCand bla. Eleven STs were identified, including ST164 from the common tern and the pandemic lineage ST38 from water samples. Closely related ST354, ST738, and ST13823 isolates were detected across different sampling periods and sites. Virulence factors associated with ExPEC/APEC and IPEC/aEPEC pathotypes were identified in six and four isolates, respectively. This is the first report of ESBL-E. coli in common terns in Latin America and reveals surface water contamination by multiple recurrent STs, suggesting anthropogenic drivers of antimicrobial resistance in this wetland ecosystem.

title: Rectal colonisation with carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales, vancomycin-resistant enterococci, ESBL-producing Enterobacterales and Clostridioides difficile in hospitalised patients: a point prevalence study
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global healthcare challenge with implications for patient outcomes, healthcare-associated infection prevention, and healthcare costs. Data regarding asymptomatic rectal colonisation with multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) among hospitalised patients in Ireland remains limited. This study assessed rectal colonisation in general wards at a large Irish tertiary hospital. A point prevalence survey was conducted across three acute wards in St James's Hospital, Dublin, in 2024. Adult inpatients with capacity to consent were recruited. Rectal swabs and/or stool samples were collected and screened for carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE), vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE), extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales (ESBL-PE), and Clostridioides difficile. Microbiological analysis included selective chromogenic agar culture, MALDI-ToF identification, VITEK2 antimicrobial susceptibility testing, lateral flow testing for carbapenemase detection, and molecular testing for C. difficile. Fisher's exact test was used for statistical analysis. Thirty patients were included in the study. No patients were colonised with CPE. VRE colonisation was detected in 33.3% (10/30) of participants with an exploratory association observed between VRE carriage and antibiotic treatment during the current admission (p=0.01). Confirmed ESBL-PE carriage was detected in 13.3% (4/30) of patients. One Enterobacter cloacae isolate demonstrated carbapenem resistance; however, no common carbapenemases were detected on lateral flow testing. C. difficile colonisation was identified in 6.7% (2/30) of patients. This study demonstrates a substantial burden of VRE and ESBL-PE carriage among hospitalised patients in Ireland, while CPE carriage remained uncommon. These findings support the importance of continued surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, and infection prevention measures to limit transmission of resistant organisms within healthcare settings.

title: An AI-designed, recombinantly produced FtsZ-directed peptide with in vitro activity against pan-drug-resistant clinical isolates
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is outpacing the antibiotic pipeline, yet antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) - the most-cited alternative class - remain constrained by proteolytic instability, host toxicity, and the cost of solid-phase synthesis. We report an integrated design-to-validation pipeline that addresses these constraints and yields a de novo peptide directed at an intracellular, non-lytic target. Instead of relying on membrane disruption, the design was directed at FtsZ, the essential bacterial cell-division GTPase, at a consensus epitope (residues 60-145) that our alignments show is substantially more conserved across the Gram-positive/Gram-negative divide than FtsZ overall (68.6% versus 50.1% identity between Enterococcus and Klebsiella orthologues) while sharing only approximately 8-24% identity with human tubulin. A sequence-space diffusion model conditioned on the amino-acid composition of experimentally validated AMPs generated ten binders; fusion to 120 cell-penetrating motifs, machine-learning triage, co-folding and replicated molecular dynamics identified a single lead, Combined111. Rather than chemical synthesis, the peptide was produced biologically: the codon-optimised gene was cloned in-house into pHT254 and expressed as an intracellular, C-terminal 8xHis-tagged product in the protease-deficient Bacillus subtilis WB800N host, giving a mean transcript induction of 3.40-fold (SD 2.01, n = 4 biological replicates) and a single band of approximately 11.1 kDa after one-step Ni-NTA purification. Against one pan-drug-resistant clinical isolate of each of seven species, the purified peptide produced larger inhibition zones than a panel of last-resort antibiotics for five of the seven, by a mean of 4.81 mm, although this difference was not statistically significant (95% CI -0.64 to 10.27; t(6) = 2.16, p = 0.074, Cohen's dz = 0.82). Each zone value is a single measurement, so reproducibility was not assessed, and inhibition-zone diameters are not a direct measure of comparative potency. The advantage was consistent in direction but not uniform, the pan-drug-resistant Enterococcus faecalis isolate being the least susceptible. E. faecium FtsZ was the sequence used for the computational design, whereas the Gram-positive organism available for experimental testing was E. faecalis. These findings show that generative design can be coupled to low-cost bacterial expression in one laboratory. FtsZ-directed inhibition is presented here as a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism: target engagement was inferred from alignment, co-folding and molecular dynamics, and no direct binding measurement, FtsZ polymerisation or GTPase assay, or Z-ring localisation experiment was performed. Minimum inhibitory concentrations, resistance selection, haemolysis, mammalian cytotoxicity, and in vivo efficacy all remain to be established.

title: Host-specific distribution of antimicrobial resistance in non-clinical Salmonella: a one health analysis of 791,298 isolates
abstract: The environmental distribution of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is frequently attributed to diffuse agricultural and aquatic reservoirs. To evaluate source-associated differences in AMR carriage, pre-computed genomic metadata for 791,298 Salmonella enterica isolates from the NCBI Pathogen Detection database were analyzed. Multivariate logistic regression, adjusted for serovar, geographic location, and database submission year, stratified non-clinical isolates into specific ecological niches against a human clinical baseline. Historical resistance (tetracycline) and mobilized colistin resistance (mcr) demonstrated profound concentration in poultry and swine environments. Crucially, while Extended-Spectrum Beta-Lactamase (ESBL) carriage was negatively associated with swine, bovine, and generalized aquatic environments, poultry isolates exhibited an over four-fold increased relative prevalence (Adjusted OR = 4.03). Conversely, general aquatic environments consistently demonstrated a negative association across all resistance classes. These findings indicate that environmental AMR carriage within this database is highly compartmentalized, highlighting direct livestock production interfaces as primary targets for genomic surveillance.

title: Reviving the antibiotic pipeline: an industrial perspective on scientific, economic, and policy challenge
abstract: The global antibiotic development pipeline is critically declining due to interconnected scientific, economic, regulatory, manufacturing, and policy challenges, worsening the antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis. The review examines the antibiotic pipeline from an industrial viewpoint, highlighting significant scientific, economic, and regulatory challenges. It proposes policy reforms and incentive models to encourage sustainable innovation and ensure equitable access to new antibiotics. Bacterial AMR was responsible for approximately 1.27 million deaths and associated with nearly 4.95 million deaths globally in 2019, notably in western sub-Saharan Africa. In the U.S., the CDC cites around 2.8 million resistant infections and over 35,000 deaths annually. Projections suggest that without action, AMR could lead to 10 million deaths per year by 2050 and result in multi-trillion USD economic losses. The review synthesizes findings from extensive literature across databases like PubMed and ScienceDirect, focusing on articles from January 2010 to June 2025, with an emphasis on high-quality evidence. The data underscore the urgent need for a comprehensive, multi-stakeholder strategy incorporating novel discovery platforms, push-pull economic incentives, adaptive regulatory pathways, and regionalized manufacturing models. Strengthening global partnerships between policymakers, funders, and industry is essential to rejuvenate the antibiotic pipeline, safeguard therapeutic effectiveness, and ensure equitable global access.

title: proMGE2-a planetary-scale resource of mobile genetic elements in microbial (meta)genomes
abstract: proMGE is a resource of prokaryotic mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that systematically catalogues MGEs from prokaryotes, their intercellular spread, antimicrobial resistance gene carriage, and MGE nesting interactions. We present proMGE2 featuring a 6X expansion, a total of >16.4 million MGEs from 670k high-quality isolate genomes, and 180k metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), spanning diverse MGE categories: transposons and insertion sequences, phages, phage-like elements, conjugative elements, mobility islands, and integrons. proMGE2 includes MGEs from MAGs derived from environmental microbiomes, encompassing ~50k samples across several major habitat types. proMGE2 provides a standardized MGE reference collection of >5 million non-redundant MGE sequences drawn from our curated database, and enables identification of MGEs in user-provided genomes. proMGE2 captures MGE diversity and their functional potential at unprecedented scale to support future research of mobile genetic elements and transfer of genetic material in microbes. The database is available at http://promge.embl.de/.

title: Respiratory Infections at Mass Gatherings: A Travel-Medicine Review with Hajj and Umrah as a Longitudinal Case Study
abstract: Mass gatherings combine international mobility with dense, repeated contact and can amplify respiratory infections across travel corridors. Hajj, Umrah and Kumbh Mela, offer a uniquely recurrent case study, while other religious or sporting mega-events, and music or cultural festivals provide contrasting exposure systems. A focused narrative review was conducted of peer-reviewed studies, systematic and scoping reviews, and authoritative public-health guidance. Searches and project evidence synthesis prioritized publications from January 2021 to August 2026, with selected foundational sources. We examined respiratory symptoms, laboratory detections, clinical disease, vaccination, antimicrobial use and resistance, surveillance, environmental modifiers, and pre-, during-, and post-travel practice. No meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias scoring was undertaken. Respiratory risk is determined less by attendance alone than by contact intensity, duration, ventilation, vocalization, shared accommodation, traveler susceptibility, and pathogen circulation. Recent Hajj evidence confirms a substantial burden of respiratory symptoms and clinical consultations, but estimates vary because denominators range from volunteers and tested samples to healthcare encounters. Rhinovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and bacterial pneumonia remain important. There is continued abuse of antibiotics for predominantly viral syndromes and acquisition of resistant organisms link individual care to global antimicrobial resistance. Syndromic, laboratory, event-based, genomic, and wastewater surveillance are complementary, not interchangeable. Heat, dust, air quality, fatigue, and differential access to protective infrastructure modify respiratory symptoms, severity, and care seeking. Comparative events share mechanisms but not directly transferable rates. Travel-medicine practice should treat mass gatherings as longitudinal exposure systems spanning preparation, transport, the event, and return. Layered vaccination, risk-based masking, ventilation and crowd-flow measures, prompt diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, and explicit travel histories, can reduce respiratory morbidity while preserving denominator discipline and access to protective infrastructure.

title: The Interrelation between Phenotypic Properties and Sequence Type in Clinical Isolates of the Klebsiella Pneumoniae Species Complex
abstract: A comparative study of the biological properties (phenotypic characteristics and sequence types) of clinical isolates of Klebsiella pneumoniae obtained from two pediatric multidisciplinary hospitals (PMH-1 and PMH-2) was carried out. All isolates exhibited high levels of antimicrobial resistance (up to 100%), including resistance to third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins, while over 70% remained susceptible to meropenem. Strains from PMH-2 demonstrated resistance to polyvalent Klebsiella bacteriophage (up to 75%) and a weak biofilm-forming capacity (84.4%). According to sequence typing data, strains with different genetic characteristics prevailed in each hospital: strains of the K2 serotype and different sequence types were detected mainly in PMH-1, whereas strains with the sequence type ST307 predominated in PMH-2. The biofilm-forming capacity, the K2 capsular type, and the presence of various sequence types determine population heterogeneity and contribute to increased drug resistance of these Klebsiella strains.

title: Chemical characterization, antibacterial activity, in vitro cytotoxicity, and selectivity of the lipid extract from Sargassum filipendula against multidrug-resistant bacteria
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria necessitates new therapeutic alternatives, and marine macroalgae represent an underexplored source of bioactive lipids. This study characterized the lipid extract (LE) of Sargassum filipendula and evaluated its antibacterial and cytotoxic profiles against MDR hospital isolates. LE composition was determined by GC-MS, and its thermal behavior by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Antibacterial activity was evaluated using the broth microdilution method (CLSI M07) against Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and coagulase-negative staphylococci, followed by determination of the minimum bactericidal concentration. Cytotoxicity was assessed in L929 and MDBK cell lines using MTT, Neutral Red, and Lactate Dehydrogenase assays; Hemolytic activity was evaluated using erythrocytes; and selectivity indices (SI) were calculated for each bacterial species. Palmitic acid (61.07%) and oleic acid (15.90%) were the predominant fatty acids. TGA revealed a total mass loss of 82% across two decomposition stages (296 °C, 445 °C), and DSC detected no phase transitions between - 80 and 270 °C. The LE exhibited bacteriostatic activity against all isolates, with MIC values ranging from 1.18 mg/mL (S. aureus) to 2.5 mg/mL (P. aeruginosa). Cytotoxicity assays yielded ICvalues ranging from 0.16 to 1.25 mg/mL, and the hemolytic ICwas 12.81 mg/mL. However, assay-specific SI values were ≤ 1.06 for adherent cells and 5.12-10.86 for erythrocytes. The S. filipendula LE is a candidate source of antibacterial compounds against MDR bacteria, although purification processes and in vivo validation are required to establish its therapeutic potential.

title: Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus: biological basis and prospects for antimicrobial application
abstract: The rapid rise of antimicrobial resistance has become a major global health challenge, particularly due to multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria with complex resistance mechanisms and strong biofilm-forming capacity. Simultaneously, conventional antibiotic development has struggled to keep pace with the increasing prevalence of resistant pathogens, prompting renewed interest in alternative antimicrobial strategies. Among these, predatory bacteria, particularly Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus and related organisms collectively termed Bdellovibrio and like organisms (BALOs), have emerged as promising biologically driven agents capable of selectively targeting Gram-negative pathogens. This review examines the biology and predatory behaviour of B. bacteriovorus in the context of its proposed application as a "living antibiotic". The evolutionary background, taxonomy, cellular organisation, and biphasic life cycle of the organism are discussed to establish a framework for understanding its predatory efficiency. Particular emphasis is placed on the molecular mechanisms involved in prey recognition, periplasmic invasion, intracellular growth, and the distinctive non-binary mode of cell division. Evidence from in vitro and in vivo studies evaluating activity against multidrug-resistant pathogens and biofilm-associated infections is critically assessed, together with current insights into host immune interactions and safety considerations. Recent advances in imaging technologies, genetic tools, and regulatory pathway analyses have substantially expanded the mechanistic understanding of Bdellovibrio biology. Beyond therapeutic applications, BALOs also demonstrate potential in agriculture, aquaculture, food safety, and environmental management. Although challenges related to large-scale production, delivery strategies, and regulatory acceptance remain, current evidence supports BALOs as promising components of future antimicrobial frameworks.

title: Alginate oligosaccharides attenuate inflammatory injury in bovine endometrial epithelial cells: Involvement of Nrf2 signaling and autophagy-related processes
abstract: Bovine endometritis is a common reproductive disorder in dairy cattle, and concerns regarding antimicrobial resistance and drug residues have increased the demand for alternative strategies. Alginate oligosaccharides (AOS) possess anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, but their protective effects against bovine endometrial inflammation remain unclear. This study investigated the protective effects of AOS and the underlying mechanism in lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-challenged bovine endometrial epithelial (BEND) cells. AOS pretreatment alleviated LPS + ATP-induced cytotoxicity, inhibited NLRP3 inflammasome activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production, attenuated oxidative stress, and improved mitochondrial homeostasis. AOS pretreatment did not significantly alter LC3-II levels but reduced p62 accumulation under inflammatory conditions, and inhibition of lysosomal degradation partially diminished the protective effects of AOS against oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Furthermore, AOS activated Nrf2 signaling and increased HO-1 expression, whereas Nrf2 knockdown attenuated AOS-induced changes in LC3-II and p62 protein levels and weakened the suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Collectively, these findings indicate that AOS protect BEND cells against LPS + ATP-induced inflammatory injury, with the involvement of Nrf2 signaling and autophagy. This study provides new insights into the cellular mechanisms underlying the protective effects of AOS against bovine endometrial inflammation.

title: Host-Directed Ferroptotic Stress Modulation Against Intracellular Bacterial Infections: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Translational Challenges
abstract: The rise in antibiotic resistance and the persistence of intracellular infections underscore the urgent need for novel antimicrobial agents and strategies. Ferroptotic stress is a cell state marked by transiently elevated Felevels, increased lipid peroxidation, and altered redox balance. It has gained significant attention due to its role in the progression of various diseases, especially bacterial infections. By inducing intracellular iron overload, disrupting the bacterial microenvironment, and activating innate immune cells like macrophages, it serves as a crucial strategy to restrict intracellular bacterial growth and limit the emergence of resistance.
